full_judgment:
9. It is the question of status of an individual. When that status is assailed by a positive case much higher degree of proof was necessary and the courts below unfortunately had overlooked this point completely. The trial court ought ret to have allowed such evidence to be led in when mere verbal statement damaging the social status of a person is being made. The entire plaintiff's evidence on this point ought to have been discarded by the trial courted the court of appeal over looked the fact that the court below had ignored the presumption of law and such presumption can only be rebutted by positive fact and not by mere assertion or ipsi dixit. It is the plaintiff who brought the suit and he took up the positive stand that the defendant is a son of one Baramoni and since this onus was not discharged the plaintiff ought to have been non-suited. Unfortunately that did not happen. The courts below have decreed the suit and we shall come to this later as to whether such suit can at all be decreed. 

 "But where there is no proof of legitimate birth or illegitimate birth and the paternity of a child is unknown in the sense that no specific person is shown so have been his father, then his acknowledgement by another, who claims his as his son, according to the authorities I have quoted from, afford a conclusive presumption that the child acknowledged is the legitimate child of the acknowledger and place him in that category" (10 All p. 317). 

 18. This proposition of law was reiterated in the case of Habibur Rahman Chowdhury vs Altaf Ali Chowdhury, 48 1A 114. It raises a presumption which may be taken advantage of by either wife-claimant or son-claimant, Being however, a presumption of fact, and not jurisdiction jure, it is, like every other presumption of fact, capable of being set-aside by contrary proof. The Privy Council says in a formula as under: 

 19. "The present case accordingly is one of an acknowledgement by the father, an acknowledgement which involves the assertion that he, the father Khurshid, was married to Musammat Babo, the appellant's mother. Such acknowledgement undoubtedly raises a presumption in favour of the marriage and of the legitimacy." (Page 206). 

 In that case, it was held, there was absence of circumstances sufficient to find or justify such a presumption or such an inference. 

 25. The lower appellate Court approached the question from another angle namely, that the plaintiff's case was that defendant Khorshed Alam is the son of one Baramoni, a reputed prostitute of Natore and that he was adopted by Johura Khatoon, the second wife of Amir Ali Mia who was a tribal lady from Siliguri. It was noticed that this onus was not discharged by the plaintiff and that Baramoni who was still alive was not adduced as a witness by the plaintiff. The appellate Courts suggests "that Baramoni as mother of the defendant could not come forward to assert her mother hood of the defendant at this stage which may doom the further of the defendant the defendant also did not produce her in supported of his case, it is the therefore well proved that the defendant is not a legitimate son of late Amir Ali" (page 194 of Paper book). The suggestion is unwarranted and the conclusion is arbitrary being contrary to all presumption of law built up over the last 150 years! The appellate court below took the view from Exhibit G the Ekramama that 'why then Amir Ali wanted to disprove Khorshed Alam from Mutwalliship as back as 1953 which was due to him if he is a real son of Amir Ali Mia." 

 26. Before proceeding further both trial court and the lower appellate court erred in law and failed to take notice of the presumption in the matter of personal status which will be considered presently. 

 29. Secondly, the Muslim dictum of acknowledgement was not appreciated by the Courts below and unfortunately the High Court Division also overlooked the settled proposition that is laid down in 6 IA page 201 that the marriage will be held proved and his legitimacy established unless the marriage is disproved. The High Court Division unfortunately mentioned that the defendant has not been able to prove the alleged marriage with Monwara Begum and concluded as such "alleged marriage of Amir Ali with Monwara has been disproved." Evidence Act deals with the concept, 'proved or not proved or disproved". Had the onus been on the defendant then the High Court Division could have said that the marriage was not proved, but the Privy Council settled that as onus is upon the plaintiff to disprove the marriage and if he establishes it, marriage is disproved. These legal concepts ate to be applied in the facts and circumstances of the cases, and any derailment by way of allocation of onus bound to cause a miscarriage of justice and the findings of fact arrived at are in contravention of the presumptions of law and therefore such finding of facts cannot stand as noticed by the Privy Council in 51 CWN Much emphasis was given by the plaintiff on Exhibit G to show that Amir Ali Mia as far back as 1953 denied Mutwalliship to Khorshed Alam and nominated that after his death the eldest son by his other wife should be the Mutwalli. Strenuous arguments were advanced by Mr Ahmed that this shows that the Mutwalli Amir Ali did not intend Khorshed Alam to be the Mutwalli. This document read as a whole belies the contention; on the other hand, Khorshed Alam was appointed as de facto guardian during the minority of the plaintiff. True that Amir Ali intended that Mutwalliship should pass on the issue of his other wife but wakf nama has not reserved such power to him which says: 

 2. Acknowledgement of Amir Ali Mia raises a presumption in favour of the defendant as to his sonship. 

 6. Social relationship with the family of Amir Ali, and Khorshed Alam and that of the plaintiff raises strong circumstance in favour of the presumption of acknowledgement inasmuch as Khorshed Alam married to first cousins one after another of the plaintiff. The affidavit of plaintiff's mother's mother (Nani) though of 1967 throws light as to how controversy arose over the Mutwalliship only for which the plaintiff went to length of denying the acknowledgement of sonship by Amir Ali Mia. 

 Shahabuddin Ahmed J : I have had the opportunity to read and consider the judgment of my learned brother, BH Chowdhury, J I very much regret that I am unable to agree with him on the views expressed and the decision arrived at in his judgment on the real question that calls for determination in this appeal. The real question is whether the presumption raised by late Amir Ali's acknowledgement that the appellant in his eldest son has been rebutted or set-aside by contrary proof adduced by the respondent an admitted son of late Amir Ali. Respondent filed the suit for this particular purpose in pursuance of this Court's earlier judgment in Civil Appeal No. 27 of 1975, reported in 29 DLR (SC) 295. Both the trial Court and the lower Appellate Court, on a concurrent finding of facts, decreed the suit holding that defendant appellant is not a legitimate son of Amir Ali, and the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division, on a revisional application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, did not find any ground to interfere with the concurrent finding of fact. Now it is to be seen whether the learned Single Judge rightly refused to interfere with the concurrent decision of the Courts below. 

 32. At the outset. I would refer to the judgment of this Court in Civil Appeal No. 27 of 1975 in order to make it clear that the principle of law governing this suit was already determined and finally settled by this Court in that appeal, and thereafter, the party interested was advised to file a suit to rebut by contrary proof the presumption raised in favour of the defendant-appellant by late Amir Ali's acknowledgement that the defendant was his son. The said appeal also related to the same dispute that arose between the appellant and the respondent on the Mutwalli ship of the "Salamat Hossain Wakf Estate." On Amir Ali's death both the appellant, Khorshed Alam, and the respondent, Amir Sultan Ali, claimed the Mutwalliship as the eldest son of Amir Ali. The Commissioner of Waqfs, later on designated as Administrator of Waqfs, provisionally accepted the claim of the respondent Amir Sultan Ali and appointed him the Mutwalli in terms of the Waqf deed treating him as he eldest son of Amir Ali, the late Mutwalli, and expressed the view that the question as to who is the eldest son of the late Mutwalli should be decided in a properly constituted suit and till that decision the respondent would work as Mutwalli. This decision, as we have seen, was act aside by the High Court Division in a previous Revisional Application and its judgment was confirmed by this Court in Civil Appeal No. 27 of 1975 and it was held that in view of Amir Ali's acknowledgement" the appellant should be prima-facie treated as Amir Ali's son and he would hold the office of Mutwalli till the presumption of legitimacy in his favour is rebutted in a properly constituted suit, in that judgment this Court observed: 

 "The Muhammadan law does not recognize legitimation, and acknowledgement cannot create or confirm the status of a legitimate son in favour of or upon a person, who as a matter of fact, is not or is disproved to be the legitimate son of the acknowledger. But in the absence of any evidence to the contrary, an acknowledgement raises a presumption, the rebuttal of which is the burden of the person who disputes it, and such a presumption can be rebutted only on the proof that the acknowledged person is not or cannot be the legitimate son of the acknowledger. The principle which seems to be well established is that an acknowledgement has the effect of raising presumption of legitimacy excepting where illegitimacy is proved beyond doubt by reason of the marriage of its parents being either disproved or found to be unlawful. Having regard to this principle the High Court came to the conclusion that prima facie, in view of the earlier acknowledgement by Amir Ali, respondent (Khorshed Alam) should be accepted as the legitimate eldest son of Amir Ali until the contrary is proved in a Civil Court of competent jurisdiction. The respondent should be treated as the eldest son and as such entitle to succeed, in terms of the Waqf deed, to the office of Mutwalli, until it is established in a properly framed suit that in spite of such acknowledgement there had been in fact no marriage between the mother of the respondent and the deceased Mutwalli." 

 "This acknowledgement raises a presumption that defendant Khorshed Alam is the legitimate son of late Amir Ali Mia and this presumption can be rebutted only on the proof that the acknowledged person is not or cannot be legitimate son of the burden is on the person who disputes, i.e. here in this case this onus lies on the plaintiff. Now let us see how far the plaintiff has been able to discharge the onus on him." 

 38. In this appeal by special leave the appellant did not take the grounds that he had taken before the High Court Division, but raised again the question of legitimacy by the acknowledgment which was already accepted as a prima facie proof of his claim to son-ship by the courts below in pursuance of this Court's previous decision. The sole duty of these courts was therefore to see if the prima facie proof was nullified and rebutted by contrary facts Leave granted was to see whether the appellants "claim to son-ship of Amir Ali is established by the acknowledgment of Amir Ali claiming the former to be his son. The point for consideration is whether the learned Judge of the High Court has correctly decided the principle of acknowledgement under Muslim Law". This question is superfluous, for in the previous decision of this Court the principle of acknowledgement under Muhammadan Law was explained, presumption of legitimacy by acknowledgement was taken in favour of the appellant and it was the respondent on whom the onus was laid to rebut the presumption by contrary proof. The question thus raised in the suit was whether the defendant was born of any valid marriage between Amir Ali and any woman claimed by him to be his mother. This was purely a question of fact which fell for determination by the Courts below. These Courts were not called upon to re-state the principle of law as to acknowledgement and its effect. The appellant, it appears, has raised the question of acknowledgement against to create a smoke screen in an attempt to escape from the adverse finding of facts, which he otherwise could not challenge. 

 39. The law applicable to the question is well settled, as already indicated by this Court in the judgment in Civil Appeal No. 27 of 1975. It is that when the paternity of a person is uncertain and another person acknowledges him as his son, then this acknowledgement is a substantive evidence of the fact that the person acknowledged is his legitimate son; such acknowledgement raises a presumption that the person acknowledged is born of a valid union between the acknowledger and the mother of the person acknowledged. But being a presumption of fact and not of juris at jure, it is like every other presumption of fact capable of being set-aside by contrary proof. Onus of such a proof is upon the person who challenges the acknowledgement. His onus may be discharged by bringing evidence that the person acknowledged is not the legitimate son of the acknowledger became he was not the offspring of any valid marriage between the acknowledger and mother of the acknowledged or because it is impossible for the acknowledger to beget the acknowledge or the marriage between him and the mother of the acknowledged is prohibited by law. In elaborating this principle it is found that to become a legitimate son on the strength of an acknowledgement the following ingredients are necessary, namely the acknowledge was born of the loin of the acknowledger, that is, the former is the descent from the latter; the age difference between them is such that the acknowledger must have attained puberty at the time he allegedly begot the son; the mother of the acknowledge was legally married wife of the acknowledger at the relevant time; the marriage between these two is not prohibited by law, that is, the wife is not within the prohibited decree in relationship. Any offspring other than from such valid union is illegitimate being the offspring of zina that is, adultery, incest or fornication. In a nutshell, a valid marriage between the parents is the essential precondition for legitimacy. If such marriage is disproved. Acknowledges case falls straightaway, and no amount of acknowledgement shall make the acknowledge a legitimate son. 

 "The rules of Muhammadan Law relating to acknowledgement by a Muhammadan of another as his son are rules of the substantive law of inheritance. Such an acknowledgement, unless certain impediments exist, confers upon the person acknowledged the status of a legitimate son capable of inheriting. Where there is no proof of legitimate birth or of illegitimate birth, and the paternity of a child is unknown, in the sense that no specific person is shown to be the father, then the acknowledgement of him by another who claims him as him son affords a conclusive presumption that he is the legitimate child of the acknowledger, and places him in that category" 

 Facts of the case related to a dispute between the appellant Allahdat Khan and his step-brother Ismail Khan over inheritance from their father Golam Ghous Khan. Ismail Khan was admittedly a son of Golam Ghous Khan through his first wife, and Allahdat Khan claimed that he was a son of Golam Ghous Khan through his another wife named Moti Begum. It was contended by Ismail Khan that Moti Begum was married to Golam Ghous Khan long after the birth of Allahdat Khan and, as such, the latter was born, as an illegitimate son of his father, Form the evidence adduced the date of Moti Begum marriage could not be ascertained with certainty. But Golam Ghous Khan had acknowledged Allahdat Khan as his son during his lifetime. In these circumstances it was held that presumption as to legitimacy by acknowledgement remained unrebutted and consequently Allahdat was held to be a legitimate son of Golam Ghous Khan. 

 42A. The crux of the instant case is whether the appellant was born of any legally married wife of Amir Ali and if the answer is in the negative his claim to sonship shall fail straight-away and the acknowledgement of Amir Ali will be of no avail and the presumption as to legitimacy raised by the acknowledgement shall stand rebutted. It is only to rebut this presumption that the suit has been brought, and weather the appellant is the offspring of any lawful union between Amir Ali and Monowara Begum whom the appellant claims to be his mother is purely a question of fact. By a concurrent finding the trial Court and the lover Appellate Court held that there was no woman like Monowara Begum but she was invented for the purpose of the suit and that Amir Ali had no wife named Monowara Begum, Now it is to be seen whether a Court exercising Revisional jurisdiction under section 115 CPC can interfere with this finding. A finding of fact is immune from revision unless is shown that the finding is based on gross misreading of evidence or on nor-consideration of material evidence or it has been founded on misconception or misapplication of law or on misinterpretation of any material document or otherwise it is perverse being contrary to evidence on record. To see whether this finding suffers from any such weakness. I would go straight to the evidence both oral and documentary adduced by both the parties. 

 46. Thereafter, from 1965 till his death in 1967, Amir Ali made statements denying that the defendant was his son but contending that he was his foster son. The plaintiff produced documents containing those statements. Exhibit 3 is a certified copy of the plain of Money Suit No. 33 of 1965, renumbered as MS No. 5 of 1966, which was filed by Amir Ali against the defendant claiming arrears of rent in respect of a part of the Waqf Estate In that plaintiff the defendant was shown as his foster son. Exhibit 7 is the plaintiff of another suit-OC Suit No. 381 of 1966, filed by Amir Ali for ejecting the defendant stating that the defendant's parentage was unknown, Exhibit 5 is Amir Ali's deposition in MS No. 5 of 1966 where he said that the defendant was his foster-son. Exhibit 1 is a petition dated 14-3-66 of Amir Ali addressed to the Commissioner of Waqf in which he stated that the defendant (Khorshed Alam) was not his son but was his foster son, that the plaintiff Amir Sultan Ali was his eldest son and eligible for appointment of Mutwalli in terms of the Waqf deed. Exhibit 1 (a) is an affidavit sworn Amir Ali on 6-3-67 in respect of his petition Exhibit 1 in which he reiterated that Khorshed Alam was not his son but was his foster son. About one month thereafter Amir Ali died and thus the struggle for succession to Mutwalliship began. It was argued in the Courts below that the question of legitimacy was raised and the acknowledgement was annulled at the instance of plaintiff's mother before Amir Ali's death. Evidence however shows that this question was raised as far back as 1933 when the defendant was a child of two years that is seven-years before the marriage of plaintiff's mother. As to acknowledgement, subsequent annulment got no legal effect. But the plaintiff has not built up his case on the annulment; he has built up his case on positive evidence of competent witnesses that the defendant was not born of any of Amir Ali's wives. The trial Court and the lower Appellate Court on consideration of the evidence found that the presumption of sonship raised by the acknowledgement has been rebutted by the unimpeachable oral evidence that the defendant was not born of any wife of Amir Ali. This finding of fact is based on impregnable mass of good evidence and appreciation of this evidence being correct and proper the finding is as strong as granite pillar, which is too strong to be dented by the fragile weapon of revisional jurisdiction. Interference with this finding in revision will be disobedience to the direction of law.
